title: Cabinet clears Rs 2,814-cr critical mineral processing scheme and Rs 17,500-cr energy storage scheme
where: Economy, page 13 (Pratyush Deep), with an Explained box on energy storage
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Industrial policy; Investment models (viability gap funding) · GS1 › Distribution of key natural resources (critical minerals) · GS2 › Government policies and interventions
summary: The Cabinet approved a Rs 2,814-crore capex scheme (30% capital subsidy) for two lithium and two nickel processing plants, and a Rs 17,500-crore viability gap funding scheme for 92 GWh of grid-scale energy storage.
evolution: To ease the energy transition, ramp up storage and strengthen transmission.
PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity goal for the next 10–11 years.
Cabinet to consider a capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing.
ideas: Processing is the chokepoint: India has little processing capacity and is almost 100% import-dependent for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon, while China dominates processing and uses it as leverage in trade tensions.
GS3 · Mineral security / GS2 · Strategic vulnerability
Mining alone is not enough: control of processing decides who holds leverage in the critical mineral value chain.

Targeted capex support: a 30% capital subsidy for two lithium plants (30 kt each) and two nickel plants (50 kt each), capped at Rs 500 crore and Rs 900 crore per beneficiary, serving EVs, battery storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Capital subsidies for lithium and nickel plants aim to build the missing middle of India's battery value chain.

Mineral-specific parks: Gujarat (heavy rare earths) and Andhra Pradesh (a rare earth corridor), Odisha for nickel (reserves, and an eastern location for imports from Indonesia), Maharashtra for lithium, each as a complete ecosystem; a stockpiling policy is also being drafted.
GS1 · Location of industries / GS3 · Mineral security
Siting each processing park where reserves, skills or import routes exist applies the logic of resource-based industrial location.

Storage closes the renewable gap: Rs 17,500 crore (2026-27 to 2030-31) for 92 GWh (30 GWh battery storage, 60 GWh pumped hydro, 2 GWh emerging technologies), equal to 170% of existing grid-scale capacity, because renewable power is abundant in some hours and short in others.
GS3 · Energy infrastructure
Energy storage turns intermittent solar and wind into dependable power, the missing link of India's transition.

Market design plus Make in India: storage capacity will be allocated through tariff-based competitive bidding, discoms are eligible for VGF, and battery projects must meet a 40% domestic content requirement, linking storage demand to domestic manufacturing.
GS3 · Investment models (VGF) / Make in India
Viability gap funding with competitive bidding and domestic content rules uses public money to crowd in private investment and local manufacturing.
keywords: Viability Gap Funding (VGF)
A capital grant that makes a socially needed but commercially weak project viable
GS3 · Investment models
VGF for storage bridges the gap between high upfront costs and affordable tariffs.
Pumped hydro storage
Pumping water uphill with surplus power and releasing it through turbines at peak demand
GS3 · Energy
Pumped hydro, two-thirds of the new storage target, is an old technology with a new role in the energy transition.
Domestic Content Requirement (DCR)
A rule that a share of a project's components be made in India
GS3 · Industrial policy
A 40% DCR ties battery storage demand to India's own manufacturing base.
Strategic stockpile
A reserve of critical minerals to guard against supply disruptions
GS3 · Mineral security
A critical mineral stockpile does for batteries what strategic petroleum reserves do for oil.
Intermittency
Variability of solar and wind output across hours and seasons
GS3 · Renewable energy
Storage is the answer to intermittency, which grows with every gigawatt of solar added.
data: India's grid-scale energy storage capacity and its target
Government of India (Union Cabinet), via IE
India has about 54 GWh of grid-scale storage against a target of 411 GWh by 2031-32: a near eightfold scale-up is needed.
examples: Odisha chosen for nickel processing
Domestic reserves plus an eastern location to process nickel imported from Indonesia
GS1 · Industrial location · GS3 · Mineral security
Odisha's nickel park shows industrial location balancing local resources with access to imported ore.
Storage VGF scheme (92 GWh)
30 GWh batteries, 60 GWh pumped hydro, 2 GWh new technologies
GS3 · Energy transition · Investment models
The Rs 17,500-crore storage VGF is a ready example of public funds crowding in about Rs 97,600 crore of investment.
pyqs: Key challenges to India's energy security; measures with growth and sustainability.
Will India meet 50% of energy needs from renewables by 2030? Role of shifting subsidies.
Status and targets for renewable energy; National Programme on LEDs.
Can regional resource-based manufacturing promote employment in India?
Multi-dimensional implications of the uneven distribution of mineral oil in the world.

trend.t: Energy questions moved from renewable targets and solar costs (2015, 2016) to whether India can meet 50% renewables by 2030 (2022) and, in 2026, energy security with growth and sustainability. Mineral questions so far asked about the distribution of resources (2021) and the environmental hazards of mining (2025).
trend.watch: Energy security was asked in 2026 (GS3) and 2025 (GS2), so it is a must-study area. The next step is likely the transition's own dependencies: storage, grids and critical minerals.
focus: Storage and grid integration of renewables
Critical mineral value chains and dependence on China
Investment models for clean energy (VGF, PLI, competitive bidding)

parts: Why storage is the missing link

answer.t: In November 2026 the Cabinet approved Rs 17,500 crore of viability gap funding for 92 GWh of storage, as India has only about 54 GWh against a target of 411 GWh by 2031-32.

answer.h: Why storage is the missing link

pts.t: Solar and wind are abundant in some hours and short in others, so supply must be shifted in time.
pts.ex: Solar peaks at noon, demand peaks in the evening.

pts.t: Storage balances sudden swings in renewable output.
pts.ex: Sri Lanka's 2026 blackout from rooftop solar disconnecting (IE, 4 Nov 2026).

pts.t: Surplus renewable power can be stored instead of wasted.
Stored power can meet evening peaks now met by thermal plants.
Storage makes the 500 GW non-fossil target usable round the clock.
Battery demand can anchor domestic manufacturing.
pts.ex: 40% domestic content rule for battery projects.

pts.t: Storage projects are capital-heavy, so tariffs are high without support.
Batteries need lithium and nickel that India imports almost entirely.
Financially stressed utilities struggle to pay for storage.
Sites, land and environmental clearances take time.
Few markets yet reward storage for balancing services.
Competitive bidding with capital support.
Processing capacity and stockpiles.
Batteries for short duration, pumped hydro for longer.
Pay for ancillary and balancing services.
Recover battery minerals to reduce import needs.

answer.t: Adding solar and wind builds India's clean power; storage makes it dependable, so the transition will move only as fast as storage does.

title: On Govt agenda: New Rs 2,800-cr capex scheme for critical minerals
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Pratyush Deep), with an Explained box
syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effects on industrial growth; Infrastructure: energy; Mobilisation of resources · GS1 › Distribution of key natural resources across the world and India · GS2 › Effect of policies of other countries on India's interests (China) · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations
summary: The Union Cabinet is likely to take up a scheme of about Rs 2,800 crore that offers a 30% capital subsidy for two lithium and two nickel processing plants, to build India's domestic critical mineral processing base.
evolution: PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity goal; storage needs batteries (energy thread).
Cabinet to consider a capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing.
ideas: The gap is processing, not only mining: India has little processing capacity and is almost fully import-dependent for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
GS3 · Industry / GS1 · Resources
India's critical mineral weakness lies in processing; mining ore is of little use without the capacity to refine it.
Concentration as a strategic risk: China dominates global critical mineral processing and has used it as leverage in trade tensions, leaving India open to supply disruptions.
GS2 · India–China / GS3 · Economy
China's hold over mineral processing turns supply chains into tools of pressure, so diversification is national security.
Capex support to start a domestic base: a 30% capital subsidy for four plants (two lithium, two nickel) aims to turn ores into high-purity compounds, with cobalt recovered from nickel.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Capital subsidies for processing plants target the costliest, riskiest link in India's mineral value chain.
Clean-energy and strategic sectors depend on it: the minerals feed electric mobility, battery storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
GS3 · Energy / Defence industry
Without lithium, nickel and cobalt, India's EV and battery ambitions rest on imported inputs.
Cluster approach: processing parks in four states, each built as an ecosystem for one mineral, backed by a planned stockpile under the National Critical Minerals Mission.
GS1 · Location of industries / GS3 · Industrial policy
Mineral-specific parks link resource geography to industry, and a strategic stockpile insures against shocks.
keywords: Mid-stream processing
Refining ores into high-purity chemicals used by battery and electronics makers
GS3 · Industry
India's critical mineral challenge is mid-stream: refining, not just mining.
Weaponisation of supply chains
Using dominance over a resource to pressure other countries
GS2 · IR / GS3 · Economy
China's control of mineral processing shows how supply chains can be weaponised in trade disputes.
Strategic stockpile
A government reserve held to ride out supply disruptions
GS3 · Economy / Security
A critical mineral stockpile works like a strategic oil reserve for the battery age.
Value-chain localisation
Building each stage of production at home
GS3 · Industrial policy
Localising the mineral value chain cuts import dependence from mine to battery.
Resource-based clusters
Industrial parks placed near the raw material they use
GS1 · Location of industries
Odisha's nickel and Gujarat's heavy rare earths show resource-based clustering in practice.
data: Allocation committed for a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme, 2024-25 to 2030-31
National Critical Minerals Mission (Government of India), via IE
The government has committed Rs 500 crore (2024-25 to 2030-31) for a critical mineral stockpile under the NCMM.
examples: Four mineral-specific processing parks
Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh for rare earths, Odisha for nickel, Maharashtra for lithium
GS1 · Distribution of resources · GS3 · Industrial policy
Matching parks to state resources (Odisha's nickel, Gujarat's heavy rare earths) is a model of resource-based industrialisation.
China's leverage over mineral processing
Dominance used as leverage in trade tensions
GS4
GS2 · India–China · GS3 · Economy · GS4 · Ethics in IR
China's use of mineral processing as leverage is a clear example of economic interdependence turned into coercion.
Odisha as a gateway for imported nickel
Eastern location suits imports from Indonesia
GS1 · Location of industries · GS2 · Act East
Odisha's eastern coast lets India process nickel imported from Indonesia, linking resources to the Act East region.
pyqs: The West fostering India as an alternative to China's supply chains.
Challenges for India as the world moves from free trade to protectionism; how to meet them.
Rationale, achievements and improvements of the PLI scheme.
Why India's mining contributes little to GDP despite its Gondwana origin.
Why mining is an environmental hazard; remedial measures.

trend.t: Mineral questions began in physical geography (resource distribution, mining's low GDP share, 2017–2022) and industrial location (2019, 2020). From 2024 the frame shifted to supply chains and geopolitics: India as an alternative to China (2024), protectionism and industrial incentives such as PLI (2025).
trend.watch: Supply-chain resilience and China-plus-one questions are rising since 2024, while mining's environmental cost was asked again in 2025. Critical minerals sit where these meet, so expect a direct question soon.
focus: Industrial policy tools: PLI, capex subsidies, parks
Resource geography and location of processing
Environmental cost of mining and processing

practice.q: "Critical minerals are to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th." Discuss India's vulnerabilities and the steps needed to secure its critical mineral supply chains.

answer.t: In November 2026 the Union Cabinet is set to consider a Rs 2,800-crore capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing, as India remains almost fully import-dependent for key critical minerals.

pts.t: Lithium, nickel and cobalt are core to Li-ion batteries for EVs and grid storage.
pts.ex: Needed for India's 500 GW non-fossil goal.

pts.t: Smartphones, semiconductors and electronics depend on these minerals.
Defence systems and speciality steels need rare earths and alloys.
Like oil, control of supply gives power over others.
pts.ex: China's processing dominance used in trade tensions.

pts.t: India relies almost completely on imports for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
Even where ore exists, India lacks refining capacity to make battery-grade compounds.
Global processing is concentrated in China, which has curbed exports of some minerals in the past.
pts.ex: Export curbs on gallium and germanium (2023).

pts.t: Large parts of India's mineral potential remain unexplored.
Processing plants are costly and technology-intensive, deterring private investment.
Mining and chemical processing can damage land, water and local communities.
30% capital subsidy for lithium and nickel plants under the proposed scheme.
A mission-mode approach to exploration, processing and overseas assets, with a planned stockpile.
pts.ex: Rs 500 crore committed for stockpiling (2024-25 to 2030-31).

pts.t: Ecosystems in four states matched to their resources.
pts.ex: Odisha for nickel, Gujarat and AP for rare earths.

pts.t: Secure supplies abroad through state firms and partners.
pts.ex: KABIL; India's membership of the Minerals Security Partnership.

pts.t: Recover minerals from used batteries and e-waste to reduce fresh demand.
Strict environmental norms and benefit-sharing with mining communities.

answer.t: Just as oil security shaped the last century, building domestic processing, diverse partners and a strategic stockpile will decide India's energy and strategic autonomy in this one.

title: Steel policy for 2047 needs to shift focus — from protection to competition
where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Montek S Ahluwalia, Shishir Gupta & Rishita Sachdeva, CSEP)
syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effect on growth; Effects of liberalisation; Mineral resources · GS1 › Distribution of industries and mineral resources; Effects of globalisation · GS2 › Government policies
summary: On the Draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047, the writers argue Indian steel is profitable because it is protected, not efficient, and that duties, quality-control orders and the iron-ore export duty must be phased down.
ideas: Big but not yet competitive: India has risen to the world's second-largest steel producer, but the draft policy's goal of global competitiveness needs a clear meaning, as high profits come from protection, not efficiency.
GS3 · Industrial policy
High profitability under protection is not the same as global competitiveness.
Cheap ore, underpaid states: a 30% export duty on high-grade iron ore keeps domestic ore far below global prices, subsidising steelmakers at the cost of mineral-rich regions and exploration.
GS3 · Mineral policy / GS1 · Resource regions
Export duties on ore transfer value from mineral-rich regions to steelmakers and discourage mining.
Protection hurts users of steel: import duties and Quality Control Orders make Indian steel costlier than even high-cost Japan, raising costs for construction, automobiles and export-oriented MSMEs.
GS3 · Industry / MSMEs
Protecting an input industry taxes every industry that uses it, especially MSME exporters.

Competition did not kill other industries: tariff cuts in pharmaceuticals and auto components were followed by rising shares in global exports; steel should cut duties to ASEAN levels over five years and drop QCOs.
GS3 · Liberalisation / Trade
Pharma and auto parts show that lower protection can raise, not reduce, export competitiveness.

Reform the structure, not just tariffs: consider privatising some public-sector plants, remove the ore export duty and overhaul mining policy that discourages exploration (explorers must surrender discovered mines to auction).
GS3 · PSU reform / Mining
Competitive steel needs privatisation of laggard PSUs and a mining policy that rewards exploration.
keywords: Infant-industry trap
Protection that outlives its purpose and blunts efficiency
GS3 · Industrial policy
Steel risks an infant-industry trap: protected long after it grew up.
Non-tariff barriers (QCOs)
Quality Control Orders that restrict imports without tariffs
GS3 · Trade
Quality Control Orders act as non-tariff barriers that raise input costs.
Effective protection
Protection of an industry net of protection on its inputs
GS3 · Trade
High effective protection for steel shifts costs to downstream users.
Downstream competitiveness
Cost advantage of industries that use an input
GS3 · Industry
Cheaper steel improves downstream competitiveness in construction and autos.
Exploration incentive
Reward to finders of new mineral deposits
GS3 · Mining
Without exploration incentives, India's geological potential stays largely unexplored.
data: Steel export target in the Draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047
The Draft National Steel Policy targets 45 million tonnes of steel exports by 2047.
Steel products under QCOs / recommended for removal by the Gauba Committee / actually suspended so far
GS3 · Trade / Ease of doing business
QCOs cover 228 steel products; the Gauba Committee reportedly recommended removing 122, but only 59 have been suspended.
examples: Pharma and auto components after tariff cuts
Lower protection was followed by higher shares in global exports
GS3 · Liberalisation · GS1 · Globalisation
Pharma and auto parts show that exposure to competition can make Indian industry globally competitive.
Quality Control Orders on steel
Rules meant for quality working as import barriers
GS4
GS3 · Ease of doing business · GS2 · Regulatory overreach
QCOs on steel show how a well-meant regulation can turn into protection and raise costs for small firms.
Iron-ore export duty
Domestic steelmakers gain while mineral-rich states earn less
GS1 · Resource regions · GS2 · Federalism · GS3 · Mining
The iron-ore export duty shows how national policy can quietly shift value away from mineral-rich states.
Jamsetji Tata, 1912
Built India's first steel plant despite British scorn, without today's protections
GS1 · Modern Indian history · Essay
Jamsetji Tata's steel plant shows Indian enterprise succeeding on capability, not protection.
pyqs: Why industrial growth lagged GDP growth after reforms, and recent industrial policy.
Challenges as the world turns to protectionism.
Manufacturing and MSMEs in faster growth.
Why mining contributes little to India's GDP.
Location of iron and steel industries.

trend.t: Industry questions moved from why manufacturing lagged after reforms (2017) and capital-intensive exports (2017) to manufacturing and MSMEs for faster growth (2023) and a world turning protectionist (2018, 2025). Geography asks about steel location (2014, 2020) and mining's low share in GDP (2021).
trend.watch: Protectionism and manufacturing competitiveness have come in 2018, 2023 and 2025. Prepare the trade-off between protecting industry and making it competitive, with sector examples.
focus: Protection vs competitiveness in industrial policy

potential: "Protection may raise profits, but only competition builds global competitiveness." Examine with reference to India's steel sector. (15 marks)
Why does mining contribute little to India's GDP despite rich mineral resources? Suggest reforms. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Protection may raise profits, but only competition builds global competitiveness." Examine with reference to India's steel sector.

answer.t: India is now the world's second-largest steel producer, and the Draft National Steel Policy targets 45 Mt of exports by 2047, yet its profits rest heavily on protection.

pts.t: Shielded the industry while it scaled up.
Steel underpins defence and infrastructure.
Protects against surges of cheap imports.
Supports jobs in steel regions.
Assured margins attracted capital.
Export duty on ore underpays mineral-rich regions.
Steel costlier than in Japan, hurting construction and autos.
Higher input prices blunt export competitiveness.
QCOs on 228 products; only 59 suspended of 122 recommended.
Profits mask inefficiency, especially in PSUs.
Mining rules discourage new discoveries.
Bring duties to ASEAN levels over five years.
As the Gauba Committee recommended.
Expose firms to global ore prices.
Privatise laggard plants with strategic oversight.
Reward explorers, as in Australia.
Lower protection went with higher export shares.

answer.t: As pharma and auto parts show, Indian industry competes best when exposed to the world; steel's road to 2047 must run from protection to competition.
